then.text: The greenshank moved their nests back from the nearest ridge. I count them every April. I will say what I counted and no more.
Same number on the ridge as last year. Same is a good number, when you have seen what different looks like.
They moved them off the deep peat, and I am a little bit cross about the ones that are left, and I have decided to be cross in a measured way.
I hear the strath has made up its mind. Whatever it is, I will be out on the ridge counting come April.
Ah. They sent you. Good, they usually send me a lawyer.

I do not oppose wind. I oppose it in the wrong place. Deep blanket bog is a bad place to build: roads and foundations cut the drainage, the peat dries, and it gives back the carbon it has held for thousands of years.

The Flats are mostly thinner ground on the south side and deep on the north. Greenshank and golden plover nest across the lot. Turbines do not kill many of them; what happens is they move off and do not come back. It is the quiet kind of loss.
The peat of the Flows holds more carbon than all the forests in Britain put together. Turbines on thin ground are a different conversation.

And I will tell you the other thing, because I would want to be told. The fund is real. A village with a leaking roof and a school bus that does not run is not an abstraction. Anyone who tells you the peat is simple is selling something. So is anyone who says the roof is.

else.text: About the wind farm on the Flats? Hear the estate manager first, he will be in the Flagstone Bar at the back. Then come and ask me what the ground is.

then.text: Our star surveyor! The survey's off to the scientists and the birds are, I'm told, unimpressed. That's how you know it's going well.
Eleven lochans, a cross greenshank and a five-metre peat core. That's a proper survey. The UNESCO folk will be delighted, and they're not easily delighted.
Take these. Bog myrtle: rub the leaves and the midges keep their distance. Mostly. It also smells lovely, and in the old days it went in the beer.

How's the survey going? Three things on the clipboard: count the dubh lochans with the Flowmoor by the trail pools, listen for the greenshank with the bird surveyor, and help the peat scientist take a core out west of the road.

else.text: Welcome to the Flow Country! Four thousand square kilometres of blanket bog, the biggest in Europe, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2024. The first peatland in the world to be given that honour.
We're doing the annual bog survey and we're short of hands. Fancy it? Count the pools, listen for the birds, help take a peat core. You'll learn more about bogs than you ever thought you'd want to.
Start at the Dubh Lochan Trail over the road. The flagstones keep your feet dry. Mostly.

then.text: Lovely weather for it! No, honestly. Rain is the whole point of a bog. Sphagnum moss can hold up to twenty times its own weight in water.

else.text: Climb the Flows Lookout over the trail and you can see for miles: pools, moss, sky, and not one single tree. People find it either bleak or beautiful. Usually both, in the same minute.
Hen harriers, merlins, red-throated divers on the lochs, otters in the burns. And the midges. Never forget the midges.
